overview.text: Michelangelo Buonarroti painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling in fresco for Pope Julius II between 1508 and 1512. The vast vault is arranged as a connected biblical program: nine central panels show stories from Genesis, from Creation through Noah, while prophets and sibyls occupy the surrounding spaces. Painted architectural framing and pairs of nude youths called ignudi help organize the scenes. The ceiling’s monumental scale, illusionistic design, and powerful, sculptural figures made it a landmark of Renaissance painting. Its creator, who considered himself chiefly a sculptor, produced one of his most celebrated painting projects here.

key_facts.text: Pope Julius II commissioned Michelangelo to paint the ceiling in 1508; the work was completed in October 1512.
The nine central panels depict Genesis stories in three groups, including Creation, Adam and Eve, and Noah.
The surrounding figures include five sibyls and seven prophets; the Met describes the sibyls as female prophets.
Pairs of seated ignudi—nude youths—flank painted bronze medallions within an illusionistic architectural framework.
Michelangelo regarded himself primarily as a sculptor, yet the ceiling was a major commission in the medium of fresco.
